subject: Accounting
title: Flexible Budgets
description: Learn Flexible Budgets in one minute.

hook.text: You budgeted for 10,000 units but sold 12,000. Is your spending over budget or in line?

buildup.text: A static budget is set once and doesn't change. A flexible budget adjusts for actual volume.

discovery.text: Flexible budgets recalculate expected costs based on real output—giving a fairer comparison.

twist.text: Without flexible budgets, a manager who sells more looks like a bigger spender—even if costs are in line.

climax.text: Flexible budgets separate volume effects from efficiency, showing where real problems lie.

punchline.text: Fair comparison requires a budget that flexes with reality.

quiz.question: What does a flexible budget adjust for?

details.summary: Flexible budgets adjust for actual activity levels, unlike static budgets that assume a single volume. This topic explains how to build flexible budgets, why they provide fairer performance comparisons, and how they improve variance analysis.
details.whyItMatters: Comparing actual results to a static budget that assumed different volume levels is misleading. Flexible budgets eliminate volume distortion so managers evaluate cost control performance fairly.
takeaways: Flexible budgets recalculate expected costs based on the actual number of units produced
They separate volume variances from spending variances for clearer analysis
Variable costs flex with volume; fixed costs stay the same in the flexible budget

faq.question: What is a flexible budget?
faq.answer: A flexible budget adjusts budgeted amounts to reflect actual activity levels. If you budgeted for 10,000 units but produced 12,000, the flexible budget recalculates expected variable costs for 12,000 units—providing a fair comparison with actual spending.

faq.question: How is a flexible budget different from a static budget?
faq.answer: A static budget is prepared for one activity level and doesn't change. A flexible budget adjusts expected costs based on actual volume. This means flexible budgets isolate whether cost overruns were due to producing more units or due to spending more per unit.
